3\.10   Jun 30, 2026  ·  Changelog

# MCPs and Organizations in Team Marketplaces

We've expanded [team marketplaces](https://cursor.com/docs/plugins) to support Team MCPs and organization groups.

## \# Team MCPs in team marketplaces

Admins can now configure Team MCP servers once and distribute them across cloud agents, the agents window, IDE, and CLI.

When an admin sets up Team MCP servers for cloud agents, they can make those same servers available in a team marketplace from **Dashboard -> Integrations & MCP** . This allows members of the team to install approved integrations locally without configuring servers themselves.

Learn more in the docs on [migrating existing Team MCPs](https://cursor.com/docs/plugins) .

Team MCP servers

## \# Marketplace access by organization group

Team marketplaces now support [organization groups](https://cursor.com/docs/enterprise/organization-groups) , in addition to team-level SCIM directory groups.

Marketplace organization groups

...

[Team marketplaces](https://cursor.com/docs/plugins) now support imports of plugin repositories from GitLab, BitBucket, or Azure DevOps so you easily add plugins and distribute them to your team.

Learn more in our [docs](https://cursor.com/docs/customize-cursor) .

3\.8   Jun 18, 2026  ·  Changelog

# Improvements to Cursor Automations

Cursor Automations save you time by automating repetitive tasks with always-on agents. This release introduces the **/automate** skill, new triggers for GitHub and Slack, and support for computer use.

## \# /automate skill

Use **/automate** to create an automation directly in your local agent session.

Describe the task you want to automate in plain language and Cursor will configure the triggers, instructions, and tools for you.

## \# An emoji trigger for Slack

React to any Slack message with a designated emoji to kick off an automation. At Cursor, we use this to trigger specific automations right from Slack.

## \# New GitHub triggers
Automations now support five additional GitHub triggers:

* **Issue comment:** when a comment is made on a non-PR issue
* **PR review comment:** when an inline comment is left on a pull request diff
* **PR review submitted:** when a PR review is submitted
* **Review thread updated:** when a review thread on a pull request is marked resolved or unresolved
* **Workflow run completed:** when a GitHub Actions workflow run finishes on a pull request or branch

We've added new templates for [triaging failed GitHub actions](https://cursor.com/marketplace/automations/triage-github-workflow-failures) and [auto-fixing PR review comments](https://cursor.com/marketplace/automations/autofix-pr-review-comments) to the [Cursor Marketplace](https://cursor.com/marketplace) to help you get started.

## \# Computer use tool for automations

Cloud agents kicked off by automations can now use their own computers to produce demos or artifacts of their work.
The computer use tool is enabled by default for every automation, just tell the agent to include a demo of its work in your instructions.

To get started, update to the latest version of Cursor. Learn more in our [docs](https://cursor.com/docs/cloud-agent/automations) .

### Improvements (3) ↓ ↑

* Automations can now be saved in an incomplete state, so you can navigate away to set up an MCP auth without losing your progress
* Automations can now open PRs by default; so you no longer have to specify that tool in the UI
* You can now delete memory files in the UI, or prompt your automation to delete outdated memories when it runs

3\.7   Jun 17, 2026  ·  Changelog

# Cloud Environment Setup and Cloud Subagents in Agents Window

This release introduces updates to [cloud agents](https://cursor.com/docs/cloud-agent) in the [Agents Window](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/agents-window) of the Cursor desktop app.

## post by Colin on May 29

Colin Community Support Engineer

10

May 29

[_Changelog_](https://cursor.com/changelog/auto-review)

* * *

You can now let your agent run longer with fewer interruptions!

Auto-review is a new run mode that lets Cursor work for longer with fewer approval prompts, while keeping execution safe. It applies to Shell, MCP, and Fetch tool calls.

Every call goes through three checks in order:
* **Allowlist:** if the call matches your terminal or MCP allowlist, it runs immediately.
* **Sandbox:** if the call can run sandboxed, it runs there with network and filesystem restrictions. Available on macOS, Linux, and Windows (via WSL2); other platforms skip to the classifier.
* **Classifier:** anything else goes to an LLM classifier, along with your current request and your [custom instructions](https://cursor.com/docs/reference/permissions) . It decides whether to allow the call, try a different approach, or surface a standard approval prompt.

The classifier adds no extra cost on top of your existing agent usage.

One thing to keep in mind: the classifier is non-deterministic and can make mistakes in both directions, so treat Auto-review as best-effort convenience, not a security boundary. For strict control, stick with Allowlist and approve calls yourself.

Set your run mode in **Settings > Cursor Settings > Agents > Run Mode,** and steer the classifier with custom instructions!
More information in our [docs](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/tools/terminal) .

[Available now in Cursor 3.6!](https://cursor.com/download)

## post by Tarek98 on Jun 8

Tarek Adel Tarek98

Feature request: bring Auto-review to the Cursor CLI

The CLI (agent) only exposes approvalMode: “allowlist” or “unrestricted” — there’s no equivalent of the IDE’s Auto-review classifier. For people running agents in Docker sandboxes, CI, or headless (agent -p) mode, this gap matters:

* unrestricted auto-approves everything (shell, MCP, fetch, file writes) with no classifier gate
* allowlist is too interactive for unattended workflows
* sandbox + unrestricted confines shell side-effects but still skips the classifier for MCP/fetch/file tools

A new approvalMode: “auto-review” in cli-config.json — reusing the existing permissions.json autoRun block for classifier steering — would close this gap and give IDE/CLI parity. The same three-step flow (allowlist → sandbox → classifier) would work great for headless/CI use cases where you want throughput without full --yolo.

results.title: Custom stores, custom tools, and auto-review for the Cursor SDK · Cursor
excerpts:
Jun 4, 2026  ·  Changelog

Changelog

# Custom stores, custom tools, and auto-review for the Cursor SDK

We've shipped a batch of new functionality across the [TypeScript](https://cursor.com/docs/sdk/typescript) and [Python](https://cursor.com/docs/sdk/python) SDKs. You can now choose how agent and run metadata is persisted, expose your own functions to the agent as tools, route local tool calls through auto-review, and nest subagents to any depth. This release also brings a set of reliability, performance, and platform fixes that make local and cloud SDK agents easier to run in production scripts, CI, and custom integrations.

## \# Custom tools

You can now hand the local agent your own tools by passing function definitions through `local.customTools` , on `Agent.create()` or per `send()` . The SDK exposes them to the agent through a built-in MCP server called `custom-user-tools` , so the model calls your code through the same path and the same permission gate as any other MCP tool.
Before this, exposing a custom capability meant standing up your own stdio or remote HTTP MCP server and wiring it into the agent. Now a function definition is enough. Custom tools are also visible to every subagent of a parent agent, so a tool you define once is available throughout the whole run.

## \# Auto-review

By default, a local SDK agent runs tool calls without asking for approval, since there's no human in the loop in a headless run. Set `local.autoReview` to route those calls through [auto-review](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/tools/terminal) instead. A classifier decides which calls run automatically and which to hold back, rather than bypassing review entirely.

You steer that classifier with natural-language instructions in [`permissions.json`](https://cursor.com/docs/reference/permissions) . The `autoRun.allow_instructions` field describes call shapes to lean toward allowing, and `autoRun.block_instructions` describes the ones to hold for review.

# IT News | Cursor 3.6 — Auto-review reduces 'y-spamming' but is not a security boundary

まるしょー｜ITニュース分析配信

まるしょー｜ITニュース分析配信

2026年5月30日 16:52

## Introduction

On **May 29, 2026** , Cursor released [Cursor 3.6](https://cursor.com/changelog/auto-review) and **Auto-review Run Mode** in their **Changelog** . This mode allows agents to call **Terminal (Shell), MCP, and Fetch** tools by passing them through a three-tier system: **Allowlist → Sandbox → LLM Classifier** , making it easier to continue execution while reducing approval dialogs.

[The Agent Security documentation](https://cursor.
com/docs/agent/security) explains that **Auto-review is the recommended default starting with Cursor 3.6** . On the other hand, the official Cursor forum ( [Auto-review Run Mode](https://forum.cursor.com/t/auto-review-run-mode/161922) ) explicitly states that because the classifier is **non-deterministic and prone to errors** , **Auto-review is a best-effort feature for convenience and is not a security boundary** .

The key points to look for are the following two:

* **Three-tier gate** — What is executed immediately, what enters the sandbox, and what is sent to the classifier or human approval
* **Confusion of terms** — **Auto-review Run Mode** (execution approval) and **Agent Review** (code diff review feature) are **different things**

\*This article is a general summary based on Cursor's changelog, documentation, forums, and publicly available information from other companies.
For decisions regarding contracts, legal, security, and auditing, please follow the latest official documentation, your company's contract and settings screens, and confirmation from experts or relevant departments. No interviews were conducted with Cursor.

* * *

## Terminology in this article

* * *

  

* * *

## 1\. What happened

The conclusion first.

* **May 29, 2026** , Cursor released **Auto-review Run Mode** as part of **3\.6** in the Changelog
* It applies to **Shell (terminal), MCP, and Fetch** tool calls
* Each call is evaluated in the order of **Allowlist → Sandbox → LLM Classifier** .
* **Settings > Cursor Settings > Agents > Run Mode** . **Auto-review is the recommended default from 3.6 onwards** ( [Agent Security](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/security) ).
* ` **.cursor/permissions.json`** allows for natural language instructions for the classifier via **autoRun** (`allow\_instructions`/`block\_instructions`).
* The official stance is that it is **best-effort** and **can be bypassed** .
**It is not a security guarantee** (docs/forum).

In a nutshell for those in a hurry,  
**the news is that while Cursor has made the Run Mode that reduces "agent y-spamming" the standard recommendation, the official team itself draws a line, stating that if strict control is required, one should choose Allowlist + manual approval or administrator settings.** .

* * *

## 2\. Key points based on official information

### 2-1. The 3-stage gate flow

[The forum announcement (Colin, May 29, 2026)](https://forum.cursor.com/t/auto-review-run-mode/161922) explains that each tool call is processed in the following order:

1. **Allowlist** — If it matches the terminal or MCP allowlist, it is **executed immediately**
2. **Sandbox** — If sandbox execution is possible, it runs with **network and file system restrictions** . Available on **macOS, Linux, and Windows (via WSL2)** . Other platforms skip this stage and go to the classifier.
3.
**LLM Classifier** — Calls that do not fall under the above are sent to the classifier with the **current request** and **custom instructions** . Choose one of **allow execution / try a different approach / standard approval prompt** .

Regarding the classifier, the forum states that **there is no additional cost for using existing agents** . **The changelog itself does not mention billing** (as of this writing).

### 2-2. The 4 types of Run Mode

[Agent Security](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/security) has the following 4 types of Run Mode.

**Before Cursor 3.6** , the docs state that the old names **Run in Sandbox** , **Ask Every Time** , and **Run Everything** were used.

**The docs explicitly state that all modes are best-effort** and can be bypassed.

### 2-3. permissions.json — Policies shareable in repositories

[permissions.json Reference](https://cursor.com/docs/reference/permissions) organizes the following.

**File locations**

* `~/.cursor/permissions.json` — Global for the user
* `<workspace>/.

...

The docs state that even if something is on the allowlist, it will still pass through safety checks, and even if it matches a block instruction, Cursor may still ask for approval.

**Priority** — **team admin (dashboard) > permissions.json > IDE settings UI** . The docs state that if an administrator controls Run Mode in Enterprise, **no additional permissions can be granted** via permissions.json or the IDE allowlist.

### 2-4. Auto-review Run Mode ≠ Agent Review

These names are easy to confuse.

Since both appear in the **Agents** section of the settings screen, it is important not to mix up **execution policy** and **code review** .

* * *

## 3\. Reading alongside other companies' moves — The same issue of 'Approval UX'

Auto-review on its own makes it difficult to see the context beyond 'one more IDE setting added.' While recent announcements from other companies are at **different layers** , they address the same issue of **approval UX for agent execution** .

### 3-1.
Anthropic — Approval fatigue and Auto Mode

[How we contain Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude) highlights **approval prompt fatigue** in Claude Code as a problem. Telemetry shows that users approve **about 93%** of prompts, and it is explained that as approvals increase, **attention to each dialog wanes** .

As a countermeasure, they introduced **OS-level sandboxing** (macOS Seatbelt, Linux bubblewrap), which they state **reduced permission prompts by about 84%** . Furthermore, in **Auto Mode** , **a separate classifier** reviews tool calls.

[Trustworthy agents in practice](https://www.anthropic.com/research/trustworthy-agents) also mentions **Plan Mode** — a UX where **the entire strategy is shown and approved beforehand** rather than individual operations.

**Cursor Auto-review** uses **IDE integration + permissions.json + 3-tier gate** , while **Claude Code Auto Mode** is **classifier-centric** .

...

**Agent 365** is for **pre-deployment and organizational registration** approval, while **Cursor Auto-review** is for **runtime approval on the developer IDE** —they are **at different levels** and are not replacements for each other. In internal policies, it is more realistic to define **both** with clear divisions of roles.

* * *

## 4\. Positioning within the Cursor product line

Recent official Cursor announcements have been progressing through **entry points, environments, models, automation, and execution policies** . Auto-review handles **execution approval for agents within the IDE** .

**Related note articles**

* **2026-05-21 (Automation)** — [Cursor — Automations expands to "agents that don't touch code"](https://note.com/marusho_1266/n/nf4c42a6b3835) ( **scheduled execution of Cloud Agents** . The Run Mode in this article is **IDE local** )

* **2026-05-14 (Environment)** — [Cursor — The environment for running AI agents becomes the main focus](https://note.

...

As a first step, it is realistic to operate with the assumption of **trying Auto-review after adding only read-only commands to the allowlist** , and if the classifier makes a mistake, **reverting to Allowlist mode** or **adding block\_instructions to autoRun** —this **back-and-forth** is expected.

* * *

## Main References

* [Cursor Changelog — Auto-review (May 29, 2026)](https://cursor.com/changelog/auto-review)
* [Cursor Forum — Auto-review Run Mode (May 29, 2026)](https://forum.cursor.com/t/auto-review-run-mode/161922)
* [Cursor Docs — Agent Security](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/security)
* [Cursor Docs — permissions.json Reference](https://cursor.com/docs/reference/permissions)
* [Cursor Docs — Agent Review](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/agent-review)
* [Anthropic Engineering — How we contain Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude)
* [Anthropic Research — Trustworthy agents in practice](https://www.anthropic.com/research/trustworthy-agents)

## Takeaways

Cursor just shipped a new run mode that tries to fix the most annoying part of working with coding agents: the endless stream of approval prompts. [Auto-review](https://cursor.com/changelog/auto-review) sits between the cautious default and the reckless run-everything mode, using a small classifier model to decide what to allow on the fly.

Auto-review is a new run mode that allows Cursor to work for longer with fewer approval prompts and safer execution. It applies to Shell, MCP, and Fetch tool calls.

results.title: Cursor Enterprise Review: Pricing, Pros, and Cons in 2026‍
excerpts:
According to user feedback and reviews from sites such as Product Hunt, G2, Reddit, and personal blogs, **these are the main pros of Cursor Enterprise:**

* **Deep codebase awareness:** Cursor can understand an entire repo structure, enabling contextually relevant suggestions and accurate refactoring across large projects.
* **Privacy mode keeps code local:** On the Pro plan, users can toggle privacy mode, but on the Enterprise plan, it’s enforced org-wide, meaning no code is ever stored or trained on by Cursor or third parties.
* **Enterprise traction:** Cursor is gaining traction among major enterprises. Notably, internal Slack polling at Amazon showed over [60 interested developers](https://www.businessinsider.com/amazon-deploy-cursor-employee-interest-spikes-ai-coding-2025-6) favored Cursor over code editors like Windsurf.
* **Centralized billing:** Instead of every developer managing their own subscription, admins can handle billing centrally through a shared dashboard.
